item.title: US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño
item.description:
Exclusive: Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river where rising water levels are a threat to safety. Is it a deliberate military strategy?

The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.

“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”

item.title: How Sudan's RSF destroyed the survivors of its el-Fasher massacre
item.description:
How Sudan's RSF destroyed the survivors of its el-Fasher massacre

Submitted by Suad Abdel Aziz on Mon, 10/26/2026 - 09:00
A year after the UAE-backed Rapid Support Forces seized North Darfur’s capital, Sudanese recount the horrors of el-Fasher and describe life now
Displaced Sudanese people who fled el-Fasher after its fall sit in the shade amid the remains of a fire at a camp in Tawila on 11 February 2026 (AFP)
Off

Three weeks ago, Hala, a Sudanese woman, left the refugee camp in Tawila and returned to the city of el-Fasher.

She took a bag and got into a small vehicle operated by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary group that took over the North Darfur capital a year ago, raping, killing and looting thousands of civilians like Hala.

When she arrived in el-Fasher, which is about 60km east of Tawila, she noticed that everything had changed. Houses had been looted or destroyed. The streets looked different.

RSF fighters immediately approached her as she got out of the vehicle. “They asked me where I was going,” Hala told the campaign group Avaaz, in an interview shared with Middle East Eye.

“I told them I was going to our family home because I needed to collect some documents, including my birth certificate and ID. They asked me how many days I was planning to stay and where exactly our house was located. They wanted to check whether I was lying to them or not.”

Hala, who used a different name for security reasons, had to describe the location of the house. She told the fighters she would need more than a day because it was a mess and she had to locate many documents. The house has no electricity, making the task harder.

'The strangest thing is that they might assault you and then tell you that el-Fasher belongs to you, that this is your home, and that you are welcome to return'

- Hala, Sudanese woman from el-Fasher

“They agreed and issued me an entry permit for el-Fasher. It was a piece of paper with my name, their signature, and the date,” Hala said.

“Dealing with them is very difficult; they can easily enter your house and threaten to rape you if you refuse to go with them. They might rape you if you refuse, beat you, and if you argue with them, you could end up in prison,” she said.

“For women, travelling to el-Fasher is extremely dangerous. Most of the people who go there are fathers and elderly people because young people's lives are at risk in el-Fasher. Even elderly people often face problems with RSF fighters,” Hala told MEE.

The day after she returned to the city, she was threatened. “Some RSF fighters saw me in the street and started speaking to me using abusive and insulting language. But there were other civilians in the street, so they did not physically assault me and eventually allowed me to return home,” Hala said.

“The strangest thing is that they might assault you and then tell you that el-Fasher belongs to you, that this is your home, and that you are welcome to return at any time. But there is no security in el-Fasher at all. Women face sexual violence, and anyone who refuses the RSF's demands can be tortured or beaten.

"I returned to Tawila, and I will never go back to el-Fasher again, even if the situation improves and life changes.”

Killing on an industrial scale

On 26 October 2025, after over 500 days of siege, the RSF launched its final offensive on el-Fasher. 

What followed was the largest single massacre to have taken place during Sudan’s war, which began in April 2023 between the RSF and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and has led to the largest humanitarian crisis in the world. 

Researchers at Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab said the speed and industrial scale of the killing could only be compared to the whole of the Rwandan genocide. 

RSF fighters, backed by the United Arab Emirates, which continues to deny its involvement, filmed themselves massacring civilians. Survivors described RSF fighters raping young women and girls, executing civilians, moving survivors to makeshift clinics to take blood from them, and exhorting ordinary people and their families. 

“In one of the streets they brought dozens of families outside the houses,” Mohamed Hassan, from el-Fasher, told MEE over the phone.

“They separated the men from the women and children. They lashed and insulted the women verbally and they fired on the men randomly. If they decided that you are a SAF or Joint Forces soldier, they will kill you immediately,” he said, referring to the allied militia fighting alongside the army.

Hanin, a Sudanese mother who escaped to Tawila, where she remains, described how she got out. “I left el-Fasher with only my daughter in my hands. I thought that once I reached Tawila, my daughter and I would finally be safe. I am still waiting for that feeling of safety to come,” she told MEE.

“I survived horrible things. There are things that happened to me that I struggle to speak about. I am a mother, and I tried to protect my daughter. I cannot explain what it does to you to see your child suffer violence and know that you could not stop it. We survived, but survival does not mean we are no longer hurting.”

Anna, an aid worker, said: “There are currently RSF prisons in el-Fasher.

“They are using old buildings as detention facilities, and the conditions of detainees are much worse than ours because they are not given food or medical care when they become sick.”

Where did everyone go?

Six weeks before the RSF took the city, roughly 107,000 had fled the capital of North Darfur. About 260,000 people were still inside the city when the assault began. Doctors Without Borders asked the question that still hangs over Sudan: where did everyone else go?

Rape, ransom and execution: The road out of Sudan's el-Fasher
Read More »

The true death toll may never be known. Monitoring groups counted at least 6,000 dead in the first 72 hours using satellite imagery, but the RSF has kept el-Fasher sealed behind a communications blackout, and human rights investigators have not been allowed in. 

A year on, bodies keep surfacing and the count is still rising. In the North Kordofan town of Bara this week, 200 mass graves were found where volunteers have recovered more than 600 bodies, most of them civilians whom witnesses say the RSF killed in the same October offensive that took el-Fasher.  

In the year since, the verdicts have come in one after another. In February, the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan determined that the RSF committed acts of genocide in el-Fasher and that genocidal intent was the only reasonable inference from its conduct. 

The US government and a string of human rights groups, including the Raoul Wallenberg Centre for Human Rights and Amnesty International, have determined that the RSF has committed genocide in Darfur.

In July, Amnesty called the atrocities perpetrated in el-Fasher “a stain on the conscience of humanity”.

Walled in

The massacre was the last stage of a genocidal process. 

The RSF besieged el-Fasher from May 2024 to October 2025, creating berms around the city to act as physical barriers trapping civilians. It shelled the city almost daily and cut off food and medicine. The World Food Programme reported that trade routes into el-Fasher were blocked and captive residents were surviving on animal fodder and food waste. 

A doctor who spent almost two years living and working inside a hospital in el-Fasher spoke to MEE about the siege.

'One of the most painful experiences for a doctor is watching a patient deteriorate when you know exactly what treatment they need but have no way of providing it'

- Sudanese doctor in el-Fasher

“Over time, the hospital became our entire world. We slept there, ate whatever food we could find and spent most of our days and nights caring for patients. For months, many of us barely saw our families,” he said.

“As the siege tightened, keeping the hospital functioning became increasingly difficult. Medical supplies stopped reaching the city, essential medicines ran out, and our equipment gradually broke down. We lost reliable access to electricity and clean water. Even finding enough food for ourselves became a daily struggle.”

Generators could only be run for two hours at night. Life-threatening emergency operations were carried out using mobile phone flashlights. Antibiotics ran out. Surgical gauze was unavailable.

“We had to improvise constantly, knowing that every compromise carried risks for our patients,” the doctor said. “Pregnant women arrived after travelling through dangerous roads, often in critical condition. We treated premature babies who depended on equipment we struggled to keep running,” he told MEE. 

“Children suffering from malnutrition and civilians wounded by shelling, as well as people with chronic diseases, were also losing access to the regular treatment they needed.

“What made everything worse was that we were experiencing the same conditions as our patients. Some colleagues became severely malnourished. Others continued working while sick or injured. We were exhausted, but there were still people waiting for treatment,” the doctor said.

“One of the most painful experiences for a doctor is watching a patient deteriorate when you know exactly what treatment they need but have no way of providing it. That happened far too often in el-Fasher.”

The cover-up

The RSF punished anyone who tried to break the blockade. Young people and traders who brought food past the berm told Human Rights Watch about deadly RSF attacks on those runs.  

Survivors spoke about the execution of people caught with supplies. During that period, a young woman, Qisma Ali Omar, was hung by her arms from a tree with her feet bound and videotaped for the world to see. 

'In Tawila every day, I see people around me getting weaker. People who were laughing and talking just days ago become too weak to stand'

- Hanin, el-Fasher survivor

When the city fell on 26 October last year, the RSF went first to the places where civilians had taken refuge. Close to 500 people were killed at the Saudi Maternity Hospital, where patients and medical staff were sheltering alongside displaced families, mostly women and children. 

UN investigators later documented mass killings at el-Fasher University and the Saudi Hospital, on the roads out of the city and at the berms built to trap its people. 

Amnesty verified videos of an RSF commander executing civilian captives. Other footage showed dozens of dead civilians in a trench that ran along the berm. The RSF spent months building the walls that became the edge of a mass grave. 

Then came the cover-up.

Between 26 October and 28 November 2025, Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab identified 150 clusters of objects consistent with human remains. Twenty showed signs of burning. Fifty-seven disappeared completely within four weeks. At the Saudi Hospital, satellites captured a pit of what appeared to be bodies burned again and again through November. 

A pile of suspected bodies beside the berm was later cleared away. The RSF tried to erase the evidence. Its leader, Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, better known as Hemedti, announced an investigation into what he called violations committed by his soldiers during the capture of el-Fasher.

Life under occupation

El-Fasher today is a city of ruins and captives. 

When a UN team finally entered in December, under close supervision, it called the city a crime scene and found few people left. One in six of those screened had severe acute malnutrition. 

Those who escaped did not escape the RSF. Survivors say the group still detains men fleeing el-Fasher and demands ransoms of up to $3,000. One monitoring group documented the detention of nearly 68,000 civilians. Tawila, once a small town, now hosts around 800,000 displaced people, most of them from el-Fasher.

'I fled to el-Fasher seeking safety. But conflict followed, forcing me to displacement again. Now, I live under a tree on a farm, exposed to the elements'

- Khadijah, Sudanese woman from el-Geneina

Khadijah is one of them. Her journey traces the RSF's path across Darfur. “I'm an elderly woman from el-Geneina,” she told MEE, referring to the city in West Darfur, where the dead were also left lying in the streets as the RSF took over in the summer of 2023. 

“I fled to el-Fasher seeking safety. But conflict followed, forcing me to displacement again. Now, I live under a tree on a farm, exposed to the elements. There is little food here, and I have no shelter. The cold is unbearable. I'm struggling to survive.”

Mudathir Mohammed Diqourni, of an el-Fasher resistance committee, warned that RSF militias are destroying farms across South and Central Darfur. 

“They are also deliberately targeting farmers, shooting and killing them as they head to their farms or attempt to protect their crops and agricultural properties,” he said.

Hunger is pushing villagers toward Tawila in search of relief. Diqourni calls this demographic engineering, an effort to drive the last residents of rural Darfur into camps or across the border “through a policy of systematic impoverishment and starvation”. 

Its most haunting image is of farmers “racing against the Janjaweed's camels in the fields” to save scraps of fodder for their own animals.

Arms networks

From el-Fasher, the RSF carried the war back east into Kordofan, and south to the Ethiopian border.

The paramilitary does not arm itself. The UN’s fact-finding mission has found reasonable grounds to believe that private companies and recruiters operating from the UAE have routed supplies through Chad and southeastern Libya, as well as Bosaso in Somalia. 

How the UAE continued supporting Sudan's RSF through Haftar and Libya
Read More »

MEE has reported extensively on this supply network and on the use of army bases in Ethiopia to assist the RSF.

These routes were used, Mona Rishmawi, a member of the UN’s mission, said, to provide “weapons, drone-related equipment, logistical assistance and personnel… to commit the atrocities in el-Fasher.” 

The US remains the UAE’s top source of weapons.

In May 2025, the Trump administration pushed $1.4bn in Chinook helicopters and F-16 parts to Abu Dhabi despite a congressional hold. In March this year, it approved more than $8bn in new weapons, drones and missiles, with billions more in sales that never had to go before Congress. 

British weaponry has been found on battlefields in Sudan and the UK government has been accused of failing to stop the el-Fasher massacre because it feared the UAE.

In Bara, the volunteers are still digging. Khadijah still sleeps under a tree on a farm. The UN has named the network that armed their killers, and Washington has named the genocide. 

“In Tawila every day, I see people around me getting weaker,” Hanin told MEE.

“People who were laughing and talking just days ago become too weak to stand. Sometimes, I wake up and learn that someone has died because they had nothing to eat.”

Hala said: “El-Fasher has completely changed. We have now reached a point where, if you want to visit your own home, you need permission from the RSF. That alone shows the situation we have reached. We just hope the war ends and things get better.” 

Sudan war
Oscar Rickett

item.title: Paris protests are not about Islam. They're about France
item.description:
Paris protests are not about Islam. They're about France

Submitted by Soumaya Ghannoushi on Fri, 10/23/2026 - 16:13
The country's crisis is deep, structural and entrenched, and it will grow more severe if the far right wins the next election
French police officers stand near a fire set by protesters during a demonstration in Montpellier, southern France, on 17 October 2026 (Sylvain Thomas/AFP)
Off

The uprising sweeping through Paris and cities across France this autumn, at times descending into violence, looting and destruction, has laid bare the depth of the crisis engulfing the country under President Emmanuel Macron. 

It is no passing outburst of anger. It is closer to May 1968, when a student revolt grew into a national upheaval whose legacy still shapes France today.

If Macron’s presidency could be defined by a single word, it would be anger. From the Yellow Vests, to the strikes against pension reforms, to the riots in the suburbs and the demonstrations of today, France has lived in a state of almost perpetual agitation. 

Macron did not create all of the country’s ills, but he has aggravated them with his arrogance and condescension towards the French people, particularly citizens of North African and African descent, and even towards France’s African partners.

The revolt is rooted in a suffocating domestic crisis: declining purchasing power, stagnant wages, rising prices and spreading poverty. Young people, along with the working and lower-middle classes, have borne the brunt, which is why protests have reached far beyond Paris. Macron’s neoliberal policies have widened inequality and hastened the decay of public services.

But the crisis runs deeper than economics. French children are taught the sacred principles of liberty, equality and fraternity. The France they then encounter is one of injustice and discrimination.

A young man named Mohammed or a young woman named Aisha may be French by birth, language and education - even third- or fourth-generation French - yet they still see applications for jobs, housing and services rejected. Integration has come to mean cultural and linguistic conformity, demanded as the price of belonging, and never quite paid in full. 

The result is generations of young citizens who speak no language but French, yet are made to feel like strangers in their own country.

Narrative of the Muslim invader

The young people who blockaded France’s high schools knew exactly what they were protesting: absent teachers, crumbling buildings, and a future poorer than their parents’ present. Yet no sooner had they taken to the streets, than others arrived to explain what they really meant.

US President Donald Trump was first. “This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!” he declared on Truth Social. He offered no evidence, and in France, no link had been established between the student movement and any religious or identity-based demands. 

Trump kept going regardless. Outside the White House, he announced that “Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon”. 

The man who presumed to diagnose the ailments of Islam now asks the Muslim world to help cure the ailments of France

The method is simple. Protesters say what they are protesting, and Trump informs them they are protesting something else. Schools, wages and the cost of living vanish. In their place stands the oldest figure in the far-right repertoire: the Muslim invader at the gates.

Then came Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who never misses an opportunity to turn Europe’s Muslims into a threat. 

On i24News, he declared that France had “succumbed to the invasion of extremist Islam” and warned that “they will devour France, they will devour Europe”. He then drew the connection that matters most to him: he claimed that after 7 October 2023, he had warned Macron that if Hamas were not eliminated in Gaza, Paris would have them too - and that this was exactly what was now happening.

This was not an outburst. It was part of a strategy, and an old one. 

In 2017, standing beside Macron, Netanyahu warned that “political Islam seeks to destroy both Israel and European countries”. He has even described Britain as an “Islamic republic”. 

The formula never changes. Collapse Palestine, migration and Islam into a single menace. Cast Israel as the front line of a civilisational war. Then tell Europeans that the Muslims among them are the enemy within.

Score to settle

The purpose is plain. If French students marching for teachers can be rebranded as Hamas in Paris, then every Palestinian flag in a European street becomes a security threat, and every protest against the destruction of Gaza becomes evidence of invasion. 

Solidarity with Palestinians is recast as extremism, and Europe’s Muslim citizens become suspects in their own countries. Fear is not a byproduct of Netanyahu’s politics; it is the product.

There is also a score to settle, and Netanyahu barely hid his glee. France has condemned the expansion of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Macron called Israel’s blockade of aid into Gaza “unacceptable” and “shameful”, and France recognised Palestinian statehood last year, infuriating Israel. 

Neither Trump nor Netanyahu was describing France. Both were campaigning. Trump was speaking to American voters ahead of the midterms, and Netanyahu gave his interview while campaigning ahead of Israel’s election. But their words land in a third campaign: France’s own presidential race, six months away.

Their narrative is Marine Le Pen’s manifesto in another accent: immigration as invasion, Islam as threat, the banlieues as enemy territory. 

Rather than confronting the causes of the revolt, Macron’s prime minister pointed at the left. Sebastien Lecornu accused ultra-left groups of having organised the violence, and charged La France Insoumise (LFI) with fanning the flames of revolt and trying to throw the country into disorder months before the presidential election. 

The charge found an eager echo: Le Pen also accused LFI of allowing legitimate social demands to be hijacked, and of seeking chaos. The centre and the far right were reading from the same script.

Nor does Macron need to blame immigrants this time. He spent years making that blame respectable. On immigration, Islam and national identity, he has too often been scarcely distinguishable from the right he claims to oppose.

Different scapegoats, same purpose: to place responsibility anywhere but where it belongs. 

Declining middle power

Muslims, migrants and the left all serve to spare the government the questions the students asked. Who let the schools decay? Who allowed purchasing power to erode? Who governed while a generation came to expect a poorer life than its parents? None of these questions is answered by Islam or LFI. All of them lead back to the Elysee.

France’s crisis does not stop at its borders. A former empire, it has become a declining, crisis-ridden middle power.

For decades after formal decolonisation, Paris preserved an extensive web of political, military, monetary and economic ties with its former colonies, particularly in Africa. This system, known as Francafrique, gave France influence far beyond what its population and economic size would otherwise have allowed.

French student protests: A generation that sees no future is rising up
Read More »

That order is now unravelling. France has been forced to withdraw its forces from Mali, Niger, Chad and the Central African Republic, and its relations with Algeria, Senegal and others have grown increasingly strained. African governments are turning instead to China, Russia, Turkey and the Gulf.

France’s crisis, in short, is not a temporary downturn. It is deep, structural and entrenched, and it will grow more severe if the far right wins the next election.

And therein lies the final irony. In 2020, Macron declared that Islam was in crisis across the world. He spoke with an air of colonial superiority, casting himself as the physician who could treat its ailments, in the tradition of the 19th-century administrators who carried “civilisation” to peoples deemed incapable of finding their own way.

Today, with France in turmoil, he has gone to the heart of the Muslim world in search of help. He spoke from Doha during a state visit to Qatar and the wider Gulf, aimed at securing France’s energy supplies amid a national cost-of-living crisis. The man who presumed to diagnose the ailments of Islam now asks the Muslim world to help cure the ailments of France. 

Perhaps the question was never who would cure Islam of its supposed crisis. It is who will cure France of its own.

The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Eye.

item.title: For Palestinians, Israeli election will only determine the pace of dispossession
item.description:
For Palestinians, Israeli election will only determine the pace of dispossession 

Submitted by Emile Badarin on Wed, 10/21/2026 - 15:54
As in settler-colonial societies across history, the real issues of indigenous rights are left off the ballot
People walk past an election poster for Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief and leader of the Yashar party, in Ramat Gan, Israel, on 15 October 2026 (Jack Guez/AFP)
Off

Israel’s general election on 27 October is widely being framed as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Polls suggest that neither Netanyahu’s bloc, nor the opposition bloc of four Jewish-led parties, will win a majority in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament. 

Arab parties, representing 20 percent of the citizenry, remain outside the arithmetic of government. Their exclusion reveals much about the political terms on which this election is being fought.  

Across history, the settler-colonial democracies that most thoroughly dispossessed indigenous peoples - the United States, Canada and Australia - have held elections that advanced this process. Because elimination and land seizures underpinned their existence, they never put these issues on the ballot; voters chose only who would do it most effectively and rapidly. 

Similarly, Israelis are not choosing a direction in the coming election. They never have. They are choosing the pace of ethnic cleansing, genocide and dispossession of the Palestinian people.

Indeed, Israel’s election campaign follows a familiar settler-colonial pattern. Voters are being asked to judge Netanyahu on wars, security, the ultra-Orthodox draft, the judicial overhaul, and other domestic issues. Yet on the questions that decide Palestinian lives, Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition offer different routes to the same destination. They may differ in intensity, pace and timing, but not in direction. 

This shared direction is forcefully reflected in the abandonment of the rhetoric of peace, negotiations and two states, which once served as a facade to conceal Israeli settler-colonialism. Dispossession is now pursued in the daylight, across the left-right divide. 

Consider Yair Golan, leader of the leftist Democrats, who dismisses the two-state solution as a “galactic leap”. 

His alternative involves more of the same Israeli settler-colonial policies: “security coordination” with the Palestinian Authority, support for its “moderate” and “effective” administrative authority, and “civil separation” between Palestinians and Israelis. Separation without equality is a euphemism for apartheid. 

Stealing land

In settler-colonial democracies across history, infrastructure has fuelled land expropriation and won votes. 

Israel has developed a similar network of legal and material infrastructure to dispossess Palestinians. The Absentees’ Property Law of 1950 has been used to transfer property rights from Palestinians forced out in 1948 to Jewish settlers and infrastructure projects. 

For decades, successive Israeli governments have classified extensive tracts of the occupied West Bank as “state land”, paving the way for colony construction and expansion.

What is at stake today is no longer simply the scope of discrimination. It is the political neutralisation of an entire constituency

Jewish-only roads, settler outposts, the apartheid wall, military zones, and projects to Judaise land in the West Bank, the Galilee and the Negev (Naqab) have been designed to displace Palestinians and expropriate their land. This has continued under virtually every Israeli government, with or without Netanyahu.

Just as settler-colonial states in the past used direct and indirect means to eliminate and dispossess indigenous peoples, Israel has pursued genocidal campaigns to drive Palestinians, who cannot vote, out of Gaza and the West Bank. This continues a pattern set in 1948, when Zionist forces massacred and ethnically cleansed Palestinians, destroying their villages and towns. 

Israel has delegated some of its dirty work to West Bank settlers. Since 2023, it has intensified a campaign to arm and shield settler militias that have been seizing Palestinian land and carrying out pogroms in Jenin, Nablus, Ramallah, Jerusalem, Jericho, Hebron and elsewhere. 

For Palestinians, none of this is a campaign pledge. It is an ongoing reality, uncontested and pursued by successive Israeli governments.  

Demographic engineering

By excluding native peoples from the electorate, settler-colonial democracies were able to guarantee that their dispossession incurred no electoral costs. On the contrary, the policymakers who facilitated it have gained public support. 

Unlike indigenous peoples in other settler-colonial states, Palestinians are not a remnant minority, but make up roughly half of the population between the river and the sea. Only a small proportion have the right to vote.  

After the ethnic cleansing of Palestine in 1948, approximately 150,000 Palestinians remained within what became Israel. They were subsequently granted a form of subordinate Israeli citizenship, which offered formal inclusion within a liberal settler-colonial state, while simultaneously denying them the right to self-determination in their homeland. Through demographic engineering, their numbers have been kept to around one-fifth of the total Israeli population. 

Netanyahu won't stop until all Arab political parties are gone
Read More »

While their citizenship entitles them to vote, Israel has neutralised the political power of their vote through a series of laws and policy measures. Since 7 October 2023, this process has intensified, with Palestinian citizens and politicians arrested, prosecuted, disqualified or expelled for expressing an opinion or liking a social media post. 

Meanwhile, the state has allowed violent crime to spiral in Palestinian communities inside Israel, with murder rates reaching record highs. Home demolitions and forced displacement have become routine in the Naqab and elsewhere. 

In 2021, Ra’am became the first independent Palestinian Arab party to join the Israeli governing coalition. It won a crime-fighting budget, recognition of three villages in the Naqab, and some municipal concessions. Land and self-determination, which the 2018 nation-state law reserves exclusively for Jews, were off the table.

What is at stake today is no longer simply the scope of discrimination. It is the political neutralisation of an entire constituency, and the wilful destabilisation of its communities.

For the indigenous peoples of North America and Australia, it made little difference who won elections. In Israel, a “liberal”, “centrist” or “moderate” government might slow the pace of dispossession and restore the facade of peace, giving western governments an excuse to look away - but it would not stop settler-colonial expansion or return a single inch of land to Palestinians.

item.title: Israel’s Netanyahu clashes with army chief over Iran-related military action: Report
item.description:
Israel’s Netanyahu clashes with army chief over Iran-related military action: Report

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Army Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir reportedly had an "unprecedented confrontation" over a proposed military operation that could trigger a war with Iran ahead of the elections on Tuesday.

According to Israeli Channel 12 reported Sunday, Zamir has resisted carrying out the military action - that remains unspecified - and requested signed documentation from Netanyahu regarding legal authorisation for it.

"This relates to an action that could lead to a flare-up with Iran, at a sensitive and dramatic moment, creating this [potential] miscalculation," a military source was quoted as saying. 

The report also cited another source that said there is military concerns that the political leadership could exploit tensions with Iran for "political benefit".

Channel 12 added that the hostility between Netanyahu and Zamir were evident at discussions on Sunday at the Palmahim Airbase, where the atmosphere in the room was described by a source as "extremely sour".
